Inscribed polytopes in curves and surfaces: a dimension count, a centring argument, and a computer-assisted certificate

Edward James Gordon aka Thor110. Preprint, working draft. Interactive companion: https://thor110.github.io/InscribedShapeProblems/. Code and data: https://github.com/Thor110/InscribedShapeProblems.

Abstract

We study four inscribed-shape problems: an equilateral triangle or a square in a Jordan curve, and a regular tetrahedron or a cube in a Jordan surface. We place them in families that continue to every dimension, and record seven results.

  1. No cubes in general. A transversality argument shows that a generic smooth closed hypersurface in contains no inscribed copy of any polytope with more vertices than the dimension of the similarity group. In particular a generic smooth, strictly convex surface in contains no inscribed cube (Theorem 1). A computer-assisted proof gives an explicit one: a cubic "egg" with rational coefficients and no inscribed cube (Theorem 1.3).
  2. Simplices in convex bodies. An elementary "centring jig" argument shows that every convex body in contains an inscribed regular simplex in every orientation that is admissible for it, and in every orientation when its boundary is (Theorems 2 and 3). For smooth bodies this is a special case of Gromov's theorem, but the proof uses only Brouwer's fixed-point theorem.
  3. Admissibility is needed. Bodies with sharp corners can lose orientations: an isosceles triangle with apex below has no inscribed equilateral triangle pointing at its apex (Proposition 5).
  4. A limit criterion for squares. Non-shrinking squares on approximations give a square on the limit (Lemma 4).
  5. A computer-assisted proof. Every Jordan curve whose polar radius stays within of that of the ellipse has an inscribed square (Theorem 6), proved in interval arithmetic. This class contains nowhere-differentiable curves that are neither locally monotone nor symmetric.
  6. The same in 3D. Every surface whose radius stays within of that of a ellipsoid has an inscribed regular tetrahedron (Theorem 7), and within in every orientation within of a given one. Within it has one in every orientation (Corollary 7.3), by a covering of all rotations with 10,544 certificates. This includes surfaces that are not , outside Gromov's theorem.
  7. Numerical studies. Four studies probe the open continuous cases:
    • on fractal curves and surfaces refined level by level, the largest inscribed squares and the tracked regular tetrahedra converge rather than shrink;
    • rectangles of 9 aspect ratios are found on all 9 test curves;
    • exhaustive counts give an odd number of squares and an even number of rectangles on every generic curve where the count settles.

Every numerical claim is reproducible from the repository, and every reported inscribed shape passes an independent check to a relative tolerance of .

1. Introduction

The inscribed square problem (Toeplitz, 1911) asks whether every Jordan curve in the plane contains the four vertices of a square. It is open. Proved cases include:

  • convex curves (Emch 1913);
  • smooth curves (Schnirelmann 1929);
  • locally monotone curves, which include all polygons (Stromquist 1989);
  • curves made of two Lipschitz graphs with small constant (Tao 2017);
  • curves close to a smooth curve relative to its curvature (Chambers 2022).

See Matschke's survey (2014) for the history. The rectangular peg problem, for rectangles of a prescribed aspect ratio, was solved for smooth curves by Greene and Lobb (2021). Vaughan showed that some rectangle always exists. The equilateral triangle, and indeed any triangle up to similarity, is inscribed in every Jordan curve (Meyerson 1980, Nielsen 1992). In , Gromov (1969) showed that every embedded sphere contains an inscribed regular tetrahedron, indeed any simplex, in every orientation. The continuous case is open. Regular octahedra are inscribed in smooth convex bodies (Makeev 2001), and cross-polytopes in smooth convex bodies in for an odd prime power (Karasev 2009). Centrally symmetric convex bodies in contain inscribed cubes (Hausel, Makai and Szűcs 2000).

The problem map. A similar copy of a polytope in has degrees of freedom, and each vertex on a hypersurface imposes one equation. So the expected dimension of the family of inscribed copies is for a polytope with vertices.

Polytope Status
Equilateral triangle 2 3 1 solved
Square, rectangle 2 4 0 open (continuous curves)
Regular -gon, 2 fails generically (Thm 1)
Regular simplex open (continuous); Thms 2–3 for convex
Cross-polytope open
Cube, hypercube false generically (Thm 1)

The square's "skeletal jig" (two perpendicular chords bisecting each other with equal lengths) generalises to the cross-polytope, not the hypercube. The tetrahedron problem generalises to the simplex. In every dimension , the only regular polytopes with non-negative expected dimension are the simplex and the cross-polytope.

Methods. The companion pages find inscribed shapes with a skeletal jig: rays from a pivot, with the target shape inscribed exactly when suitable ray lengths agree. They combine a centring iteration (the "rattle"), Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt solves, and continuation across refinement levels. Every reported shape is checked independently: its pairwise vertex distances against the target's at the best-fitting scale, and the distance of each vertex to the curve or surface, both relative to the shape's size, must be below .

Complete line-by-line proofs of Theorems 1–3, Lemma 4, Proposition 5 and Theorems 6–7 are in the appendix (the repository's PROOFS.md). Sections 2–5 state the results and give the key steps.

2. Generic non-existence

Theorem 1. Let be a polytope with vertices. For a residual set of (Whitney topology), the zero set contains no inscribed copy of .

Key steps.

  1. The similar copies of form an embedded -dimensional submanifold of the space of -tuples of distinct points.
  2. Put in the multijet space . It has codimension , which is larger than , the dimension of the domain of the multijet .
  3. By the multijet transversality theorem, for generic the multijet is transversal to , so it misses entirely.

Openness of convexity and of the radial-graph condition near then gives:

Corollary 1.1. There are smooth, strictly convex surfaces in , arbitrarily -close to the round sphere, with no inscribed cube.

Symmetric surfaces have cubes, as Hausel–Makai–Szűcs predict, but they form a meagre set, so this does not conflict with Theorem 1. Theorem 1 does not name a surface. One can be named and checked:

Theorem 1.3. The surface (inside ) is a smooth, strictly convex sphere with no inscribed cube.

The proof is computer-assisted, in interval arithmetic.

  • First, the surface is checked to be a strictly convex sphere, with and Hessian norm at most .
  • Taylor's theorem then shows that a cube with all its vertices on it would be nearly flat unless its edge is at least .
  • A branch-and-bound search over centre, size and orientation, with the orientations reduced by the cube's 24 rotations, excludes every other cube: 63 million boxes, under a minute.
  • An independent re-implementation with Arb's ball arithmetic agrees. In a control run on the ellipsoid (asymmetry 0), the search correctly finds that surface's cube.

3. Simplices in convex bodies: the centring jig

Let be a simplex whose circumcentre is interior, the unit vectors from the circumcentre to its vertices, and with . The vector spans the space of linear relations among the . For a convex body , let be the length of the -th arm of the jig at , i.e. how far stays in . The rattle field is A zero of forces , i.e. equal arms, which is an inscribed copy of .

Theorem 2. If is strictly convex with boundary, has a zero in the interior. Hence contains an inscribed copy of , in particular a regular simplex, in every orientation.

Key steps.

  1. Continuous arms. Each is continuous; strict convexity is used here.
  2. Inward at the boundary. at every boundary point; the boundary is used here.
  3. Zero. An inward-pointing continuous field on a convex body has a zero, by Brouwer applied to .

Theorem 3. Let be any convex body. Call an orientation admissible if from every boundary point some arm of the jig points into the interior of the tangent cone. Then contains an inscribed copy of in every admissible orientation. If is , every orientation is admissible.

Key steps. Apply Theorem 2 to smooth, strictly convex outer approximations (Schneider). Admissibility prevents the inscribed simplices from shrinking to a boundary point. A limit of the non-shrinking simplices is inscribed in .

Proposition 5. An isosceles triangle with apex angle below has no inscribed equilateral triangle with a vertex pointing at the apex along the axis. The bound is sharp.

So "every orientation" genuinely fails for non-smooth bodies, which is the phenomenon Gromov's hypothesis rules out. In the plane some orientation always works (Meyerson).

Why the square needs more. A square's jig has a two-dimensional relation space (, ). So the centring step yields only a rhombus, and the equal-diagonal condition requires varying the rotation. That intermediate-value step is where non-convex curves break the argument. The same happens for the cross-polytope in every dimension.

4. A limit criterion and what counting cannot do

Lemma 4. Let uniformly, with a Jordan curve. Suppose infinitely many have inscribed squares whose opposite vertices lie at parameter distance at least . Then has an inscribed square.

For generic smooth curves the number of inscribed squares is odd, and the number of rectangles of any other fixed aspect ratio is even. Section 6.3 confirms both numerically. On rough curves small squares multiply at every scale, and in the limit their number is infinite. So a proof for continuous curves has to control the sizes of squares, as in Lemma 4, not their number.

The computation takes under a second (node tools/certify-square.js), and runs live on the companion page. An independent re-implementation in Python, using the interval arithmetic of the mpmath library and sharing only the box definition, confirms it (tools/verify_certificates.py), as does a third in C with the Arb library (tools/verify-certificates.c). Only IEEE 754 arithmetic (, each correctly rounded) and about 300 lines of code are trusted.

Corollary 6.1. Let . The curve has an inscribed square, and so does for every continuous .

The curve lies outside the classical cases:

  • it is nowhere differentiable (Hardy);
  • it is not locally a graph in any direction, since a monotone coordinate would make differentiable almost everywhere, so it is not locally monotone;
  • it has no reflection or point symmetry.

Theorem 6's neighbourhood is times wider than for this ellipse. We do not claim that no other smooth reference curve brings Corollary 6.1 within Chambers' theorem. The certificate's value is that it is explicit, checkable, and reaches a rough class directly.

Tetrahedra on rough surfaces. In 3D, fix the tetrahedron's orientation, with unit vectors from its centre to its vertices; an exactly orthogonal rational rotation (a Cayley transform) keeps them exact. The unknowns are the centre and circumradius , and the equations are . The vertices do not depend on the surface, so a radial perturbation of size moves by at most , and the degree lemma applies with .

Theorem 7. Let be the ellipsoid with semi-axes . Every surface with has an inscribed regular tetrahedron (in a fixed orientation) with circumradius at least . If , it has one in every orientation within of that one.

The computation (node tools/certify-tetra.js, seconds on 4 cores) checks the 8 faces of the 4D box () in adaptive cells. Each cell is checked at its centre, with an explicit bound for the change across it, and split only if the margin is too small for its size. All 997,168 cells pass both conditions of the degree lemma with . A uniform grid would need 64 million samples for the weaker . An independent Python/mpmath implementation reaches the same 997,168 cell decisions.

Turning the tetrahedron by an angle moves by at most , which acts as one more perturbation. That gives the open set of orientations.

Corollary 7.3. If , the surface has an inscribed regular tetrahedron in every orientation.

Write rotations as unit quaternions, with Cayley vector . The tetrahedron's symmetries are the 24 Hurwitz units, and every rotation is equivalent under them to one whose Cayley vector lies in the octahedron . That octahedron is covered by 10,544 cubes of half-width . Within a cube of half-width , the vertices turn by at most . So the certificate at each cube's centre, with that turning counted as an extra perturbation, covers the whole cube. All 10,544 certificates pass (8.26 billion cells, 108 minutes on 4 cores). The covering is re-checked in exact arithmetic, and a random sample of 100 cubes in C with Arb.

With , the surface is not , so Gromov's theorem does not cover it, but Theorem 7 does.

A negative result. The same method fails on a self-similar Weierstrass blob . Taking the -octave truncation as the base curve, the certifiable perturbation is about of the remaining tail at every tested:

tail certifiable
2 0.145 0.026
3 0.103 0.023
4 0.073 0.014

Each octave shrinks both quantities by the same factor. A certificate of this kind needs a base curve whose square is robust at a scale larger than the remaining roughness. A curve with self-similar roughness at a fixed relative size never provides one. This is a quantitative form of the difficulty of the open case.

6. Numerical studies

All studies run in the browser (pages/inscribed-study.html) and from the command line (node tests/run-study.js all). Raw data are in data/.

6.1 Square shrinkage on fractal curves

Four fractal families are refined level by level with a fixed seed, so the levels converge uniformly to a limit curve. At each level, squares are continued from the previous level and searched for afresh.

Family, roughest level Edges Largest square / width
Koch snowflake, level 7 49,152 0.910 (unchanged since level 4)
Minkowski island, level 5 131,072 1.017
Weierstrass blob, level 14 131,072 0.829 (steady from level 11)
Random coastline, level 16 65,536 0.832 (0.83–0.85 since level 10)

The tracked squares change size by less than 1% per level at the highest levels. This is the hypothesis of Lemma 4, observed for finitely many levels.

6.2 Tetrahedra on fractal surfaces and rectangles of every aspect ratio

Sixteen regular tetrahedra, started at fixed orientations, are followed on three fractal surface families up to 16 octaves:

  • Weierstrass-type, Hölder exponent ;
  • ridged;
  • Hölder exponent .

The smallest tracked tetrahedron changes from to , to , and to (circumradius divided by mean radius) between levels 8 and 16. Some tetrahedra are lost along the way, through pair annihilation or tracking failure.

Rectangles with aspect ratios from to were found on all 9 test curves, in all 81 cells. On the ellipse, the search finds exactly one square and two rectangles of every other ratio.

6.3 Parity

A grid search with Newton refinement, repeated on finer grids until the count stabilises, enumerates every inscribed square and rectangle. Over 44 curves and levels:

  • the square count settled in 38 cases and was odd in all of them, from 1 up to 171;
  • the rectangle count settled in 34 cases and was even in all of them.

Signed counts vanish, because a square's two diagonals carry opposite signs. Counts fail to settle on non-generic curves (circles, long parallel edges) and on rough curves, where small squares appear at every scale.

7. Open problems

Problem Status
Square in every Jordan curve open
Rectangle of every aspect ratio in every Jordan curve open; smooth case solved
Regular simplex in every Jordan sphere open; case solved (Gromov); convex case in admissible orientations, and a neighbourhood of one ellipsoid, in every orientation within 0.02 (Thm 7, Cor 7.3), here
Cross-polytope in every (smooth convex) sphere open in general
Cube in every Jordan surface false (Theorem 1), with an explicit egg (Thm 1.3); true for centrally symmetric convex bodies

Two directions follow from this work:

  • Larger certified neighbourhoods. Theorems 6–7 could start from other smooth base curves and surfaces, use several boxes, or replace the linearisation by a higher-order model.
  • Wider 3D certificates. Second-derivative bounds for the signed distance would enlarge Theorem 7's neighbourhood, and a finer covering of the rotations would give every orientation for a wider neighbourhood than 0.02.

Theorem 1 — generic non-existence

Theorem 1. Let be a polytope with vertices. There is a residual set (Whitney topology) such that for every , the zero set contains no inscribed copy of .

We use . Let be the open set of -tuples of distinct points. Then , and

  • Immersion. is the orbit map of the smooth diagonal action of on . Orbit maps have constant rank, and an injective constant-rank map is an immersion (constant rank theorem).
  • Homeomorphism onto its image. Choose affinely independent vertices . Given , is the unique affine map with . Solving for it is linear algebra, so depends continuously on .

So is an embedded submanifold of of dimension .

Step 2: the bad set. Let . It is a submanifold of dimension in a manifold of dimension , so

Step 3: transversality forces emptiness. For in the residual set given by the Multijet Transversality Theorem, . The domain of has dimension . If , which is exactly , a transversal map cannot meet at all: at an intersection point the image of the differential (dimension ) plus would have to span a space of dimension , which is impossible.

Step 4: conclusion. Suppose contained an inscribed copy . Then and for all , so , contradicting Step 3.

Corollary 1.1 (no inscribed cube in general). There exist smooth, strictly convex surfaces in , arbitrarily close in to the round sphere, that contain no inscribed cube. Hence the conjecture "every closed Jordan surface contains an inscribed cube" is false.

Proof. Let , whose zero set is the unit sphere. The set of satisfying all of the following is open in the Whitney topology, hence in , and contains :

  1. on a small ball around the origin, and outside a large ball;
  2. on the closed annulus in between;
  3. wherever , the Hessian of is positive definite on .

(For , take the balls of radius and : then on the annulus, and the Hessian is .) For , conditions 1 and 2 make each ray from the origin cross exactly once and transversally, so is a smooth radial graph, a smooth sphere. Condition 3 gives it a positive definite second fundamental form, so it bounds a strictly convex body (Hadamard). with the Whitney topology is a Baire space, so the residual set of Theorem 1 (with the cube, ) is dense, and contains points arbitrarily close to .

Corollary 1.2. By the same argument, generic smooth Jordan curves contain no inscribed regular -gon for (). Generic smooth closed hypersurfaces in , , contain no inscribed hypercube (). And generic smooth closed surfaces in contain no inscribed icosahedron or dodecahedron.

Theorem 1.3 (an explicit egg with no inscribed cube). Let and , the repository's lopsided egg (semi-axes about , , , with no symmetry). Then is a smooth sphere bounding a strictly convex body, and no cube has all eight vertices on .

So the cube analogue of the square peg problem fails for an explicit, smooth, strictly convex surface, and not only for unnamed generic ones.

  • Part 2: no small cubes. Let a cube of edge have its vertices on , and let .

    • At the other end, the cube's diameter (with ) is at most 's diameter, and its centre, the average of its vertices, lies in 's bounding box.
  • Part 3: no other cubes. Write a cube as centre , half-edge and rotation .
    • Orientations. The cube's 24 rotations are the 48 units of the binary octahedral group: , , and for distinct . As in Corollary 7.3, every rotation is equivalent to one closest to 1 among these units. Its Cayley vector satisfies (from and the like) and (from the Hurwitz units).

Checks.

  • Control. With the asymmetry set to 0 (-DE_NUM=0), the surface is an ellipsoid. That is centrally symmetric, so it has inscribed cubes (Hausel–Makai–Szűcs). The search then fails exactly where it should: around the cube with centre 0 and half-edge . So the program finds cubes when they exist.
  • Independent check (tools/egg-cube-arb.c, about 10 minutes). A second program, in C with Arb's ball arithmetic, shares no code with the first. It bounds boxes differently: it evaluates the vertices and directly on balls of parameters, instead of using a Lipschitz bound. It redoes all three parts: 367 million boxes, all excluded. Its own control (./egg-cube-arb control) finds the ellipsoid's cube.
  • Margin. The method has room to spare. With the asymmetry reduced to or , the proof still goes through in about half a minute.

Remarks.

  • Theorem 1 is non-constructive: it shows that counterexamples are everywhere, but not where. Theorem 1.3 gives one explicitly. Before it was proved, two independent solvers found no cube on the egg closer than 1.5–2.8% of its size.
  • Symmetry is not generic. A centrally symmetric surface has inscribed cubes (Hausel–Makai–Szűcs 2000), and so, numerically, do mirror-symmetric ones. Symmetric surfaces form a small (meagre) set, so this does not contradict Theorem 1.
  • Theorem 1 says nothing about shapes with . For those, the count only says solutions are expected; existence needs a separate argument, such as Theorem 2.

Remarks.

  • Every orientation. The family of solutions is parametrised by , of dimension . This matches the expected dimension in the table.
  • Pivot only. The finders' Pivot only mode is exactly Theorem 2: it fixes and searches only over .
  • Where it stops. Strict convexity is used in Lemma A, and in Lemma B. The same happens for the cross-polytope in every dimension. For simplices nothing is missing: the centring step alone forces regularity.

Theorem 3 — every convex body

Let be a convex body (compact, convex, non-empty interior), not necessarily smooth or strictly convex. Let , and be as in Theorem 2, and for write . The tangent cone of at is , the directions into from .

Definition. The orientation is admissible for if at every boundary point , at least one arm direction lies in the interior of : from every boundary point, at least one arm of the jig points strictly into the body.

Lemma 4 — a route to the open square problem

Lemma 4. Let be a Jordan curve and uniformly. Suppose there is such that for infinitely many , has an inscribed square with two opposite vertices at parameter distance . Then has an inscribed square.

Proof. Let , which is positive because is injective and the set is compact. For large , , so those squares have diagonal at least . Their vertex parameters lie in the compact ; pass to a convergent subsequence . Uniform convergence gives . A limit of squares whose diagonals are bounded below by is a non-degenerate square, so the four points form a square inscribed in .

How the experiments relate. For the fractal families in this repository, the level- polygons, with their natural parametrisations, converge uniformly to the limiting fractal curve. The square shrinkage study finds, at every computed level, verified squares whose diagonal is at least about 0.8 of the curve's width, with their size settling as grows. That is exactly Lemma 4's hypothesis, observed for finitely many . A proof for a given fractal would need it for all .

Why counting alone cannot do it. For generic smooth curves the number of inscribed squares is odd (Schnirelmann's argument: as the curve deforms, squares appear and disappear in pairs unless one shrinks to a point), while rectangles of any other aspect ratio come in even numbers. The square-count study confirms both on smooth and polygonal curves. On rough curves, small squares multiply at every scale and the count stops being meaningful, and in the limit it is infinite. So any proof for continuous curves must control the sizes of squares, as in Lemma 4, not just their number.

Theorem 6 — a computer-assisted certificate

Theorems 2 and 3 need smoothness or convexity. Lemma 4 needs control at every level of a fractal. This section takes a third route, which handles genuinely rough curves: prove that a square cannot be removed by any perturbation of a given size. Then compute, rigorously, that the size is large enough to cover a fractal.

Let be the ellipse with , with polar radius . For a continuous , the curve is a Jordan curve: every ray from the origin crosses it once.

Interval arithmetic and what is trusted. Each operation is computed with IEEE 754 round-to-nearest, which is within half a unit in the last place of the exact result. The result is then widened outward by , which is at least one unit in the last place, so the exact result always lies inside. No other library functions are used (JavaScript does not specify the accuracy of Math.sin, Math.cos, …): the ellipse has a rational parametrisation, and the constants , and are enclosed in intervals because they are not binary fractions. What remains trusted is the JavaScript engine's IEEE arithmetic and the code itself (about 300 lines in pages/interval.js and pages/certify-rigorous.js), which is short enough to audit or port to a verified interval library.

Independent check. tools/verify_certificates.py re-implements every check from scratch in Python, using the interval arithmetic of the established library mpmath instead of pages/interval.js. It shares only the box definitions , , , which the degree lemma allows to be arbitrary. It confirms Theorem 6 in full (the same 80,000 samples; , degree margin , diagonal ). It also confirms Theorem 7 in full, with the same adaptive cells: the same 997,168 cells, none failing, with the same margins and circumradius . A third implementation, tools/verify-certificates.c, does the same in C with the ball arithmetic of Arb (FLINT 3). It reaches the same results, including the same 997,168 cells, in about 4 seconds.

Corollary 6.1 (fractal curves). Let , so . Then the curve has an inscribed square, and so does for every continuous with : random phases, Brownian-like noise, and so on.

For (the curve on the Square Certificate page), this curve is outside the classical cases:

  • Not smooth or Lipschitz. is nowhere differentiable, by Hardy's theorem, since .
  • Not locally monotone. The curve is not locally a graph in any direction anywhere, so Stromquist's theorem does not apply. If a coordinate of were monotone on some interval of , it would be differentiable almost everywhere there (Lebesgue). Dividing by the smooth, non-vanishing factor away from one point would then make , and so , differentiable almost everywhere.
  • Not symmetric. is symmetric about but not under , and is symmetric about and . So the curve has no reflection or point symmetry, and the symmetric-curve results of Nielsen and Wright do not apply.

Chambers (2022) proves that a Jordan curve close enough to a curve has an inscribed square, with closeness measured against for the maximum curvature of . For , and , so Theorem 6 covers a neighbourhood about times wider. We have not ruled out that some other smooth , with smaller curvature, lies within Chambers' bound of every curve in Corollary 6.1. So we claim only a computer-assisted proof of a quantitative statement, not a new class of curves.

What did not work: the Weierstrass blob. The method was also tried, in an earlier floating-point version (tools/certify-float.js), on the Weierstrass fractal of the finders, . The base curve is the -octave truncation, and is the size of the remaining tail, :

tail to cover best certifiable ratio
2 0.1451 0.0256 5.7
3 0.1026 0.0230 4.5
4 0.0726 0.0139 5.2

The ratio does not improve with . Each added octave shrinks the tail by , but it also makes the base curve rougher at a finer scale, and the certifiable margin shrinks at the same rate. So the blob cannot be certified this way. (The exact signed distance used now gains little: 0.141 → 0.143 for the ellipse, far short of a factor of 5.) The ellipse works because a large, smooth base square survives a fixed-size perturbation; a curve whose roughness carries a constant fraction of its size at every scale does not offer one. This is the quantitative form of the difficulty in the open problem.

Theorem 7 — the same for tetrahedra on rough surfaces

The inscribed-tetrahedron problem is open exactly for non-smooth surfaces: Gromov's theorem needs . Theorem 6's method extends to 3D if the tetrahedron's orientation is fixed, and the degree lemma of Step 2 applies unchanged with .

These are the directions from the centre to the vertices of a regular tetrahedron.

Corollary 7.1 (rough surfaces). Let be any continuous function. For example, take for a fixed unit vector , which is nowhere differentiable along every meridian through (Hardy). Then the surface has an inscribed regular tetrahedron. Such surfaces are not , or even Lipschitz, so Gromov's theorem does not apply. We know of no published result that covers them, but, as for Theorem 6, the claim is a quantitative computer-assisted one and not a new structural class.

Corollary 7.3 (every orientation). If for all , then has an inscribed regular tetrahedron in every orientation.

This is the analogue, for these rough surfaces, of Gromov's "every pose" theorem for spheres.

Proof.

  • Orientations as quaternions. Every rotation is for a unit quaternion , determined up to sign. When , the Cayley vector gives as the matrix in Theorem 7. The tetrahedron's 12 rotational symmetries are for the 24 Hurwitz units . For example, is the half-turn and permutes the coordinates cyclically, and each permutes the . So and give the same four directions , in a different order, and it is enough to prove the result for one .

Write . The units give , so and the Cayley vector of lies in the solid octahedron . It is therefore enough to cover .

Checks.

  • python3 tools/verify_certificates.py orientations re-checks the covering in exact rational arithmetic, without the JavaScript's bookkeeping. The coordinates bounding the certified cubes form a grid, and every cell of that grid that meets lies inside a certified cube.
  • ./verify orientations re-checks a seeded random sample of 100 cubes (node tools/certify-orientations.js --sample 100) in C with Arb. It takes only each cube's corners, its centre and the box data , , , and recomputes the rotation, the allowance, the circumradius range and every cell itself. All 100 pass: 81 million cells, about 3.5 minutes.
  • Re-checking all 10,544 cubes in Arb would take about 6 hours on 4 cores. It has not been done.

Why only ? Turning within a cube costs of the allowance, and the box for a general orientation has less room than the one tuned for Theorem 7. A finer grid would leave more room for , at about 8 times the cost per halving of .

Remarks.

  • The degree lemma needs no winding numbers and works in any number of unknowns. It only needs the equations to stay away from zero, and either close to their linearisation or closer to it than to zero, on the boundary of a box.
  • The neighbourhood is smaller than in 2D (0.13 against 0.15) because the tetrahedron equations are more curved relative to the box. At the degree condition fails, so is about as far as one box goes.

What remains open

Problem Status
Square in every continuous Jordan curve (Toeplitz) Open. Proved for convex (Emch), smooth (Schnirelmann), locally monotone (Stromquist) and small-Lipschitz (Tao) curves
Rectangle of every aspect ratio in every continuous Jordan curve Open. Proved for smooth curves (Greene–Lobb) and extended to rectifiable curves; some rectangle always exists (Vaughan)
Regular tetrahedron / simplex in every continuous Jordan sphere Open. Proved for spheres in every pose (Gromov 1969); Theorems 2–3 give elementary proofs for every convex body and, in admissible orientations, every convex body. Theorem 7 certifies every surface within 0.13 of one ellipsoid, and Corollary 7.3 every orientation for every surface within 0.02. "Every pose" fails for non-smooth bodies (Proposition 5)
Regular octahedron / cross-polytope Open. Proved for smooth convex bodies in (Makeev 2001) and in for an odd prime power (Karasev 2009)
Cube / hypercube () False in general (Theorem 1), with an explicit strictly convex surface that has no inscribed cube (Theorem 1.3). True for centrally symmetric convex bodies in (Hausel–Makai–Szűcs 2000)
